name: Brain Computer Interfaces
title: Brain Computer Interfaces
answer: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read electrical or chemical signals from the nervous system and translate them into commands for a computer, a prosthetic, or a communication aid, and in some designs write information back into the brain through stimulation. In this atlas they sit within neuroinformatics and the AI Physician, where they are treated as a class of medical AI rather than as consumer gadgets. The scope covers invasive implants, such as microelectrode arrays placed on or in the cortex, and non-invasive setups using scalp electroencephalography. It also includes bidirectional systems that combine recording with stimulation for movement, speech, or mood disorders. The atlas tracks these alongside 1000 medical AI models, though BCIs are only one part of that wider set.

sections.body: Brain computer interfaces are systems that read electrical or chemical signals from the nervous system and translate them into commands for a computer, a prosthetic, or a communication aid, and in some designs write information back into the brain through stimulation. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: A typical BCI runs on a chain of sensors, amplifiers, and processors that must move data from the body to a decoder with very low delay. Invasive systems rely on implanted electrode grids or arrays connected to a small external or subcutaneous unit, while non-invasive systems use EEG caps or headbands. The recorded signals are digitized and streamed to a local computer, an edge device, or a hospital server, where the decoding software runs. Many research BCIs still depend on wired connections and technician support, but clinical and home-use designs are moving toward wireless and battery-powered hardware. The compute load is modest by modern standards, but reliability, sterilization, and power management dominate the engineering.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The core work is neural decoding: turning noisy, high-dimensional brain signals into a stable estimate of what the user intends. Practitioners first record calibration data while the person imagines or attempts a movement, then train a classifier or regression model to map those signals to cursor positions, speech units, or prosthetic commands. Feature extraction often reduces the signal to band power, spike rates, or time-frequency patterns before the model sees it. Because neural signals drift from day to day, decoders are retrained or adapted continuously, and closed-loop systems add a stimulation policy that adjusts based on the decoded state. The method is less about building one large model and more about maintaining a personalized mapping between a specific brain and a specific device.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: BCIs raise distinct rights and risk questions because they collect intimate neural data and, in invasive form, place hardware inside the body. Informed consent must cover device lifetime, data storage, and the possibility that the implant may need removal or may stop working. Neural data are increasingly treated as sensitive health information, and several jurisdictions are debating whether they deserve stronger protection than ordinary biometrics. Product liability is a live concern: the atlas tracks six active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, and BCI makers face similar exposure if a device fails or causes injury. The atlas also lists 210 compliance and regulation pages relevant to medical AI, reflecting the patchwork of device, data, and research rules that BCI teams must navigate.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving from laboratory demonstrations toward longer-term, at-home use for people with paralysis, speech loss, or severe motor impairment. Wireless implants, improved electrode materials, and self-calibrating decoders are likely to reduce the need for constant expert supervision. Closed-loop stimulation for epilepsy, Parkinson's disease, and psychiatric conditions is expanding the definition of a BCI from a read-only interface to a therapeutic loop. Standards for neural data formats, interoperability, and clinical trial endpoints are still immature, and their development will shape how quickly new systems reach patients. The atlas will continue to track these systems as they move from the 805 scientific models and 1000 medical AI models now catalogued into regulated clinical practice.
